title: The UK's Investment Shortfall
gist: Oxford Economics, commissioned by a consortium of UK infrastructure owners (Manchester Airports Group, London Gatwick, Getlink, Eurostar, GIIA and others), finds the UK has under-invested versus the G7 for 25 years to the tune of ~£1.9tn cumulative, leaving it with the G7's smallest productive capital stock relative to GDP. The gap is concentrated in business investment in long-lived physical assets, and is pinned on business property taxes, delivery costs and policy unpredictability; converging to the G7 average by 2040 would lift real GDP 1.7% permanently.

themes.theme: Scale of the UK investment gap

insights.claim: Had the UK invested at the G7 average rate since 2000, cumulative UK investment would have been around £1.9 trillion higher, according to Oxford Economics benchmarking of total and business investment over 2000-2025.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Quantifies the size of the structural capex hole that any UK growth thesis must either assume gets filled or price as a permanent drag on trend growth.
insights.quote: Had the UK invested at the G7 average rate since 2000, cumulative investment would have been around £1.9 trillion higher
insights.locator: The report benchmarks UK total and business investment

insights.claim: The UK's productive capital stock is now the smallest in the G7 relative to GDP, the accumulated result of at least a quarter of a century of investing less than almost every comparable economy.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: A thin capital base caps UK supply-side capacity, arguing for structurally lower UK productivity growth and reinforcing the case for underweighting UK domestic cyclicals versus peers absent policy change.
insights.quote: the UK’s productive capital stock is now the smallest in the G7 relative to GDP
insights.locator: The report benchmarks UK total and business investment

insights.claim: The UK's investment shortfall is broad-based but concentrated in business investment — the only component whose gap with the rest of the G7 has actually widened over 2000-2025.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Points the diagnosis at corporate capex incentives rather than public spending, so watch business-rates and capital-allowance policy rather than headline government investment totals for the real signal.
insights.quote: the shortfall is broad-based but concentrated in business investment – the only component whose gap with the rest of the G7 has widened
insights.locator: The report benchmarks UK total and business investment

insights.claim: The UK's investment deficit sits in long-lived physical assets rather than intangibles, meaning the country's weakness is in buildings, plant and infrastructure rather than software and IP.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Reframes the common 'the UK is fine because intangibles are mismeasured' rebuttal; the beneficiaries of any catch-up would be construction, engineering, grid and transport asset owners, not software.
insights.quote: in long-lived physical assets rather than intangibles
insights.locator: The report benchmarks UK total and business investment

insights.claim: Three features consistently set the UK's investment environment apart from peers: the burden and design of recurrent taxes on business property, the cost of delivering and operating new capacity, and policy unpredictability.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Gives a three-part checklist for judging whether any UK Budget measure is genuinely investment-positive; measures that fail all three are noise for UK capex-exposed equities.
insights.quote: the burden and design of recurrent taxes on business property, the cost of delivering and operating new capacity, and policy unpredictability
insights.locator: Drawing on evidence from the IMF, OECD, Bank of England

insights.claim: Recurrent taxes on business property are singled out for their design as well as their level, implying that a revenue-neutral business rates reform could still lift UK investment.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Sets up a cheap policy option ahead of the Autumn Budget: watch for structural rates reform, which would disproportionately benefit property-heavy UK sectors such as retail, logistics and infrastructure.
insights.quote: the burden and design of recurrent taxes on business property
insights.locator: Drawing on evidence from the IMF, OECD, Bank of England

insights.claim: Policy unpredictability is treated as a first-order cause of weak UK capital formation on par with tax and delivery cost, because investors must have confidence in the environment over the whole life of a long-lived asset.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Implies UK regulatory-regime stability is itself a valuation input for airports, rail concessions and utilities — repeated policy resets raise required returns even when headline tax rates are unchanged.
insights.quote: improve confidence in the environment over the life of an asset
insights.locator: The report does not prescribe a programme of reform

insights.claim: In an Oxford Economics Global Economic Model scenario where UK business investment converges on the G7 average by 2040, real GDP ends 1.7% above baseline, the productive capital stock is 8.7% larger, and real household disposable income is 2.1% higher — about £1,540 per household.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Sets an upper bound on the macro payoff from UK investment reform: 1.7% of GDP over 15 years is real but modest, so avoid pricing UK capex reform as a growth regime change.
insights.quote: Real GDP ends the period 1.7% above baseline, the productive capital stock is 8.7% larger, and real household disposable income is 2.1% higher – around £1,540 per household
insights.locator: Using the Oxford Economics Global Economic Model

insights.claim: The gains from closing the UK's investment gap are characterised as permanent rather than cyclical, because they come through a larger capital stock and higher supply capacity rather than a demand boost.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Supply-side gains do not carry the usual inflation cost, so a credible UK investment revival would be a rare growth impulse the Bank of England need not lean against.
insights.quote: with the gains permanent rather than cyclical
insights.locator: Using the Oxford Economics Global Economic Model

insights.claim: Oxford Economics deliberately declines to prescribe a reform programme, instead offering a three-part test for judging proposals: whether they raise the return each pound of investment can earn, lower the cost of delivering it, or improve confidence over the life of an asset.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: A portable screen for scoring Budget and planning announcements quickly, separating genuine capex catalysts from headline-grabbing measures.
insights.quote: whether they raise the return each pound of investment can earn, lower the cost of delivering it, or improve confidence in the environment over the life of an asset
insights.locator: The report does not prescribe a programme of reform

insights.claim: The report was published ahead of the UK Autumn Budget, with the Government weighing its response to the business rates call for evidence and the implementation of recent planning, grid and energy-cost measures.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Names the near-term catalysts to watch — the business rates response plus planning, grid and energy-cost implementation — as the decision points for UK infrastructure and property capex.
insights.quote: It was published ahead of the Autumn Budget, as the Government weighs its response to the business rates call for evidence
insights.locator: It was published ahead of the Autumn Budget

insights.claim: The study was commissioned by a consortium of the UK's largest private infrastructure investors and operators — Manchester Airports Group, London Gatwick, Getlink, London St Pancras Highspeed, Eurostar and the Global Infrastructure Investor Association — signalling coordinated pre-Budget lobbying by transport infrastructure owners.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: The sponsor list reveals which owners feel most squeezed by UK property taxes and delivery costs, and flags where regulatory relief would land first if the lobbying works.
insights.quote: On behalf of a consortium of the UK’s largest private infrastructure investors and operators
insights.locator: On behalf of a consortium of the UK's largest
